claims.text: The target alloys are Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm3.
The initial non-equilibrium alloy has a largely homogeneous solid-solution structure.
The initial alloy has a fine distribution of constituent elements.
Controlled thermal aging induces Mg segregation from the matrix.
Controlled thermal aging precipitates Mg-rich intermetallic compounds from the initially homogeneous solid solution.
Mg-rich precipitates provide preferential nucleation sites for a Mg-rich oxide during high-temperature exposure.
Oxide nucleation on the Mg-rich precipitates promotes coalescence into a continuous oxide film.
The continuous Mg-rich oxide film is protective and improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Aged samples will form more uniform and adherent high-temperature oxide scales than as-processed samples.
Aged samples may exhibit lower oxidation weight gain than as-processed samples.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates create electrochemical potential differences relative to the surrounding matrix.
Electrochemical potential differences between the precipitates and matrix establish localized galvanic couples during aqueous exposure.
Localized galvanic coupling increases room-temperature corrosion relative to the as-processed state.
The phase-evolution pathway and resulting behavior depend on aging temperature, aging time, alloy composition, and processing route.
